Full text

Abstract

To increase coordination in areas of science where collaboration can benefit knowledge generation, collaborative work must also provide incentives for individual researchers to participate. This study investigates the reasons for forming large-team collaborations and the individual-level outcomes associated with participating in these projects in psychology. Through a qualitative analysis of 500 papers, we find that large-team collaborations are most often formed to address practical challenges inherent in complex research questions, although they can also serve broader social or strategic functions. A quantitative analysis of 1,699,489 papers published between 1975 and 2024 shows that large-team papers receive more citations and are published in journals with greater citation prestige than smaller-team papers. Large-team papers also receive more citations within the first two years after publication, indicating greater early citation impact. These differences are also apparent within individual researchers' publication records, with their larger-team papers tending to receive more citations than their smaller-team papers.

Overall, our findings suggest that large-team collaboration can help researchers address the resource and coordination demands of complex research while also being associated with publication and citation outcomes that are currently rewarded within academia.

The Benefits of and Motivations Behind Large-Team Coordination in Psychology Introduction

Science increasingly faces questions for which individual teams are poorly equipped (Klug & Bagrow, 2016; Leahey, 2016). To successfully address these questions, researchers need to coordinate to manage interdependencies, whether temporal, logistic, financial, or epistemic (Rasti et al., 2026). In many fields, coordination has emerged in what is referred to as large-team collaboration, which can provide researchers with access to a larger pool of resources, such as funding, human resources, complementary skills, and social capital (Lee et al., 2015).

Several of these long-term coordinated research efforts have led to impressive scientific progress, from the discovery of the Higgs Boson at CERN (European Council for Nuclear Research, Aad et al., 2012), to a consistent focus on patient-reported outcomes in rheumatology at OMERACT (Outcome Measures in Rheumatology, Tugwell et al., 2007), and complete and accurate modelling of the climate system at WCRP (World Climate Research Programme, Sommeria & Touzé-Peiffer, 2019). Psychology has also increasingly adopted such collaborative approaches, particularly following large-scale replication initiatives such as Many Labs and the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (Klein et al., 2014; Open Science Collaboration, 2015).

Yet the collective epistemic benefits of coordination do not necessarily imply that participating in large-team science is beneficial to individual researchers. This distinction is important as the current reward structure in academia places considerable weight on traditional metrics such as citation counts and the prestige of the journal. The use of these metrics as indicators of scientific quality (Aksnes et al., 2019) and metrics worthy of reward and recognition (Declaration on Research Assessment, 2012) has been challenged. Yet, they still can influence decisions about hiring, promotion, funding, and professional recognition. This poses a challenge for the uptake of coordinated projects, as they require researchers to invest scarce time, expertise, and resources, while potentially reducing autonomy and distributing scientific credit among a larger number of co-authors. Sustaining large-scale coordination may therefore depend partly on whether these investments also generate benefits on metrics that are currently rewarded for the careers of researchers who make these contributions.

Existing research provides only partial answers to these questions. A growing body of literature shows that, across different fields, papers produced by larger teams tend to receive more citations (Bikard et al., 2015; Hsiehchen et al., 2015; Larivière et al., 2015; Porter et al., 2012; Uzzi et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2019; Wuchty et al., 2007). For example, Wuchty et al. (2007) reported that mean citations for team-authored work in the Social Sciences received twice as many citations as single-authored work in the field, and self-citation only slightly reduced this effect (to 1.9 times as many citations). Similarly, Larivière et al. (2015) analyzed more than 4 million papers in Social Sciences and Humanities, and reported that the average citation of papers with 45 authors was more than 4 times as high as those of single-authored papers (the citation metric was normalized using the average number of citations received by papers in the same year and specialty). They also found that self-citations only accounted for approximately 20% of the citations for groups with between 25 and 40 authors. This pattern has also been observed in psychology, where large-team papers receive more citations and greater attention from news outlets and social media than papers with fewer authors (Coles, 2024; Coles et al., 2026). Coles et al. (2026) reported that within psychology, papers with between 30 and39 authors received 9.63 times as many yearly citations compared to papers authored by 1 to4 authors, and that such papers receive 16.32 times more mentions in news per year.

However, existing studies have largely examined these associations at the level of papers, often using a particular threshold to distinguish large from smaller teams (e.g., +2 in Wuchty et al. (2007), +10 in Wu et al. (2019)). This leaves open the question whether the citation advantage associated with larger teams is also apparent within individual researchers' publication records and how citation outcomes vary across the broader distribution of team sizes. Beyond the question on social benefits of large-team papers, an outstanding question is how epistemic reasons for large-team collaborations (i.e., different interdependencies) are visible in the papers produced by them. For example, do people collaborate to perform expensive projects, collect data that is logistically impossible in a smaller team, or do they examine questions that require more expertise than a single person can acquire? Jones (2021) reported that teams benefit from more diverse expertise and more creative idea combinations. Iglič et al. (2017), by surveying Slovenian researchers, reported that pooling resources and requiring more diverse expertise are among the reasons that promote collaborations. Yet, we do not know to what extent interdependencies motivate such large-team projects.

We address both social and epistemic questions using a large-scale bibliometric analysis of psychology publications. We first examine how citation impact varies across team sizes, including citation counts within the first two years after publication. We then extend previous work in two ways. First, we compare researchers' own larger-and smaller-team publications, allowing us to examine whether the association between team size and citation impact is also apparent within individual researchers' publication records. Second, we examine where the citation impact typical of larger-team papers falls within the citation distribution of smaller-team papers, providing a distributional perspective on the magnitude of these differences. Finally, we examine whether larger-and smaller-team papers differ in the citation prestige of the journals in which they are published, both across papers and within individual researchers' publication records.

We complement these analyses by qualitatively examining the types of projects for which psychologists form large teams and the reasons for coordination at this scale. Guided by the conceptual model of Rasti et al. (2026) we investigate whether coordination arises from logistic, financial, temporal, or epistemic interdependencies, while also identifying motivations that extend beyond these practical requirements. This analysis clarifies when large-scale coordination is currently perceived as necessary or desirable. Together, these analyses move beyond asking whether large teams produce highly cited science, and provide novel insights into why researchers coordinate at this scale, and whether doing so is associated with benefits that could 120 help sustain individual participation in collectively valuable research. 1 121 [Comments] 7 1 Although we used a similar data source to Coles et al. (2026) (both studies used OpenAlex data), our overlap with their work is limited to the use of total citation counts.

We employed a different definition of time-corrected citations and focused exclusively on English research articles. In addition, we included the field of Decision Science, which contains many psychology-related publications. Our qualitative analysis also goes beyond topic classification by examining the interdependencies that motivated the formation of large-team projects. For more information, check the method section.

Method

Our analysis used more than 1.5 million psychology papers from the OpenAlex data snapshot from October 17, 2024 (Priem et al., 2022). OpenAlex is an open-access scholarly metadata resource launched in 2022 as a successor to Microsoft Academic Graph. All data processing and analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.1 and higher, R Core Team, 2025).

OpenAlex stores all scholarly documents including journal articles within the works entity. We iterated over the snapshot's works section and retrieved all entries in which Psychology or Decision Science appeared as the primary or secondary field. Field assignment in OpenAlex is largely automated: a large language model (LLM) infers topics from the title, abstract, journal name, and citation network, and then maps topics to the most likely field using an algorithm developed by CWTS (OpenAlex, 2024). The OpenAlex team acknowledged that automated assignment can produce errors. Accordingly, we included Decision Science in adittion to Psychology, as our initial checks showed that this field in OpenAlex contains many psychology-related articles, including the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, which is a seminal large-team science project in psychology (Open Science Collaboration, 2015). We then filtered out non-psychology items by title and journal-name keywords (e.g., "symposium", "table of content", "Synthesiology", and "Aerospace"). During the qualitative analysis we identified more keywords to add to the list of records to remove, and reran all analyses (full list of keywords can be found in the Supplementary Materials). Figure 1 shows the preprocessing and data cleaning steps.

Figure 1

Data Cleaning Process Note: Retrieving the OpenAlex data from the secondary field of papers introduced noise into the dataset. The LLM model OpenAlex has used to categorise papers to fields is less accurate for the secondary field. As a consequence, we screened the data at multiple stages and developed keyword-based rules to improve the efficiency of dataset cleaning. The sample size for the first screening stage was chosen pragmatically and was further complemented by the random checks as part of the qualitative analysis. The keywords identified during manual screening were used to develop systematic filtering rules for the dataset. As individual keywords could match multiple records, we could identify a larger number of potentially irrelevant records.

Where keyword-based filtering was insufficient to identify irrelevant records reliably, we used journal ISSNs or individual OpenAlex IDs to facilitate their removal. More information about data cleaning can be found in the supplementary material and in the code file r_scripts/02_data_cleaning.R available in the paper's repository.

Metrics of Interest

To measure citation impact, we use (a) total citation counts, (b) second-year citation counts, and (c) publication-date-corrected citation counts. We chose not to adjust for selfcitations for two reasons. First, we lacked reliable self-citation data for all papers in the dataset.

Second, based on our own prior observations, large-team papers often bring together many of the field's active scholars (e.g., ManyPrimates) and produce results that serve as reference points for an entire research line. Discounting self-citations would therefore risk understating the field-level impact that is central to the current study. However, we tested the impact of self-citation on a subset of the data. In this document, analyses use second-year citation counts; robustness analyses with the other metrics (i.e., total citation and publication-date-corrected citation) are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

We operationalized the impact of journals using the SCImago Journal Rank (SJR). SJR is an open-access journal-ranking metric based on the citation impact of papers published in a journal, similar to other widely used journal-level metrics such as the Journal Impact Factor, but offers broader coverage (31,125 journals vs. 22,249 journals in Web of Science). SJR divides all citations to a journal by all documents published by the journal over a specific time window.

Unlike the Impact Factor, SJR weighs citations by the prestige of the citing journal, which is estimated via a PageRank algorithm on the journal citation network, and discounts self-citations.

Although excluding self-citations may underestimate a journal's true prestige, we relied on SJR because we could not identify alternative open-access metrics that capture journals' ranking. For comparison, in 2024, Nature had an Impact Factor of 48.5 and an SJR of 18.288 and Psychological Science had an Impact Factor of 5.1 and an SJR of 2.5. Despite greater coverage, only 1177572 records in our dataset had matching journals in the SJR records. Therefore, all results based on journal prestige are based on this subset.

Team size

In this paper, we did not impose a single threshold for large-team papers. Wherever possible, we analyzed the full distribution of the number of co-authors. We grouped papers into single-, two-, three-, four-, and five-author papers, and for the remaining papers we exploratively analyzed alternative bin widths of 5, 10, and 15 authors. In each team-size bin, the final bin captured very large teams (>100 authors); except for the 10-author scheme, where the last bin began at ≥ 96 authors to preserve 10-author intervals. In the remainder of this document, we report results using a bin width of 10 authors; robustness checks with other team size definitions are provided in the Supplementary Materials and reveal that bin size does not matter for the main conclusions.

Qualitative checks

We randomly selected 1000 papers with 20 or more authors for our qualitative analysis of the types of interdependencies that motivate researchers to collaborate. We chose 20 as the cutoff for large-team projects because pairwise comparisons of citation counts showed that papers with more than 20 authors have consistently higher mean citation ranks than papers by smaller teams (see Supplementary Materials).

Our goal was to code 500 valid records, while at the same time using the qualitative checks to identify papers that did not meet the inclusion criteria of this study. We analyzed 669 papers in total using MAXQDA 2022 software for the first round (version 22.1.0, VERBI Software, 2021) AND Microsoft Excel in the final round. From the 169 papers that did not meet the inclusion criteria, we distilled keywords that were used in the second round of data cleaning (see Figure 1).

We used a combined deductive and inductive coding approach. The initial codebook was informed by the four types of interdependence identified by Rasti et al. (2026): logistic, financial, temporal, and epistemic interdependencies. During an initial round of coding, we allowed additional reasons for large-team collaboration that were not adequately captured by these predefined categories to emerge from the data. The authors iteratively discussed these cases and refined the definitions, inclusion criteria, and examples associated with each code until consensus on the final codebook was reached. Previously coded papers were subsequently reassessed using the final codebook. Papers could receive more than one interdependency; however, interdependency codes and codes reflecting additional reasons for collaboration were mutually exclusive.

To assess coding reliability, the second and third authors each independently coded a randomly selected 10% of the final sample (50 papers each; 100 papers in total) using the final codebook. After the first batch of 50 papers, inter-coder reliability was checked. Reliability can be computed in two ways. Per criterion (e.g., did both coders assign or not assign the category 'logistic'). Although in some categories the agreement was more than 90%, the mean agreement across all categories was 70.29 percent. The second calculation can be based on whether each coder assigned exactly the same set of categories (e.g., both coders assign 'logistic', 'financial', and 'epistemic'), where the agreement was quite low at 32 percent. We, therefore, adjusted the codebook and specified rules for all categories in more detail. The second batch was coded afterward with the finalized codebook and led to the mean inter-coder agreement of 83.43 percent for criterion agreement and 60 percent for all-category agreement. The main reason for imperfect agreement was unclear reporting in the papers, which required coders to make assumptions. Disagreements, all of which involved edge cases, were discussed among the authors and resolved through consensus. Following the reliability assessment, the first author coded the remainder of the sample using the finalized codebook. More details on reliability assessment and agreement at the code level are available in the Supplementary Materials.

Coding was primarily based on the abstracts. Coders additionally consulted the Methods section when 1) the abstract provided evidence for only one code, to determine whether any forms of interdependence were evident elsewhere in the paper; 2) it was unclear whether the study involved original data collection or re-analysis of existing data; or 3) the sample size could not be determined from the abstract. For cases with no clear reason for large-team collaboration, the author-contribution statement was also consulted when available.

Results

Practical challenges are the main reason for starting large-team collaboration

Figure 2 visualizes the interdependencies identified in the large-team science papers in our sample. Among the four types of interdependency, logistic and financial interdependencies were the most frequent, identified in 295 and 225 papers, respectively. Logistic and financial interdependencies often co-occur (i.e., in 105 papers) because collecting large sample sizes often combines both.

Papers were coded as involving logistic interdependency when they involved data collection across multiple sites; resource-intensive data collection (e.g., fMRI or data collection from primates); systematic reviews with more than 100 papers at the screening stage; secondary analyses combining data from multiple sources; or bibliometric and meta-scientific analyses with samples substantially larger than is typical for such research. Financial interdependency primarily captured studies in which the required sample size was sufficiently large to make the project resource-intensive. For quantitative research, this included studies with more than 100 participants from non-general populations (e.g., people with specific disorders), more than 1,000 participants from general populations in online studies, or more than 200 participants from general populations in in-person studies. For qualitative studies, we used a threshold of 100 participants. These numbers were selected arbitrarily and based on authors' expectations of the sample sizes within the field.

Selecting a threshold, despite its limitations, was necessary as it helped to resolve discrepancies that existed in the earlier version of the qualitative analysis. Epistemic (111 papers) and temporal (92 papers) interdependencies were less frequent. Epistemic interdependencies included complex clinical trials requiring expertise beyond what would typically be available to a single researcher; explicitly multidisciplinary research, or other research projects requiring multiple domains of specialized knowledge (e.g., combining physiological and psychological interventions); skills requiring extensive training (more than four years; e.g., conducting diagnostic interviews); and the development of research tools or the proposal or revision of guidelines. Papers were coded as involving temporal interdependency when they included multiple data-collection time points (e.g., cohort or longitudinal studies and randomized controlled trials with follow-ups at least 3 months apart), multistage consensus development, or multiple sequential research stages within the same paper, such as developing and testing an instrument or conducting an original study and its replication. Importantly, our categories were designed to capture interdependencies that could be identified from a single published paper. Consequently, our temporal category captures somewhat different cases from those described by Rasti et al. (2026), because temporally interdependent stages of a research project do not necessarily appear within the same publication.

We also identified a category of papers that were part of a larger coordinated study or consortium. These papers typically reported secondary analyses of data previously collected as part of a single cohort or a larger randomized controlled trial. Large and complex studies can produce datasets with substantial informational value that can subsequently be used to address research questions beyond those examined in the original study. However, as it was not always possible to determine the extent to which the interdependencies involved in the original study were inherited by the secondary analysis, we kept these papers as a separate category.

Large teams were also present in papers for which we could not identify the types of research interdependency described above. One category comprised papers in which the large number of authors appeared primarily to serve a consensus or signalling function rather than to enable resource-intensive empirical research. These included position papers, perspective pieces, commentaries, non-systematic reviews, event or workshop reports, and papers proposing research roadmaps. In such papers, the inclusion of many authors may indicate broad support for a position, consensus around a perspective, or representation of a larger research community. We therefore classified these papers separately.

Finally, in a small number of cases, we could not identify a clear reason for the inclusion of more than 20 authors. These papers did not meet the criteria for any of the other categories, and the Methods and, where available, author-contribution statements did not provide further clarification. This does not necessarily imply that no interdependencies were present. It is possible that financial, logistic, temporal, or epistemic interdependencies existed, but they were not clearly enough communicated in the published paper to be identified using our coding procedure. Alternatively, norms of a specific field may require the inclusion of all members of a group, rather than only those who directly contributed to the paper, which may be the case for some of the papers in this category.

Figure 2

Motivations for large-team science papers

Large-team science is an increasing phenomenon

In line with previous research (Coles et al., 2026), we found an increased frequency of large-team papers in Psychology (see Figure 3). Over the last decade, the number of papers with more than 20 authors increased dramatically, and in some cases had more than double the growth rate of articles with up to 20 authors.

Figure 3

Growth of published papers across different team sizes

Larger teams receive more citations

Overall, bigger teams receive more citations (𝜌𝜌 = .223, CI = [0.221, 0.224]) 2 . This relationship is slightly stronger for the second-year citation count (𝜌𝜌 = .285, CI = [0.283, 0.286]) and slightly stronger for publication-date-corrected citation count (𝜌𝜌 = .316, CI = [0.314, 0.317]).

Analyzing papers in bins of 10 authors, the median and mean of the second-year citation counts increased fairly consistently up to the 45-author group, followed by many fluctuations (see Figure 4). For example, papers with 4 authors received, on average, 30.19 fewer citation (or when analyzing median citation rates, 5 fewer citation) in the first two year than papers with 36-45 authors. This suggests that projects with larger author groups have a relatively large [Comments] 19 2 Due to the large sample size (N = 1699489 for citation measures and N = 1177572 for journal ranking), all reported correlations are significant, with p < .001.

immediate recognition, as would be expected when researchers in a field come together to study a topic they all believe should be addressed at this time.

Figure 4

Team size and citation counts

Self-citation cannot explain the higher citations in larger teams

To test whether self-citation may impact the results, we drew a random sample of 500 papers with 20 or more authors and a random sample of 500 papers with fewer than 20 authors.

Using the OpenAlexR package (Massimo et al., 2024), we derived how many citations at the time of this search were authored by one or more authors from the original author list. Smallteam papers had a lower proportion of self-citations than large-team papers (estimated proportion: 5.75 vs. 11.72; OR = 0.46, p < .001, CI = [0.35, 0.61]). However, excluding selfcitations did not eliminate the difference in citation counts between large-and small-team papers (W = 0.46, p < .001, HL = 7, CI = [6, ∞). This shows it is unlikely that self-citation alone accounts for the observed citation difference between smaller and larger teams. Note that self-citation information was available only for total citations; we therefore could not conduct the corresponding analysis for citations received within the first two years after publication.

Larger teams are published in higher-ranked journals

The rank correlation between number of authors and SJR value (𝜌𝜌 = .167, CI = [0.165, 0.169]) is smaller than the correlation with citation count reported above. Here, papers with 4 authors appear in journals that are, on average, 1.42 lower in rank score compared to papers with 36-45 authors, and the median rank score is 0.73 lower. Figure 5 shows that mean and median SJR value increase consistently until the 46-55 authors bin, and then fluctuate for larger groups.

Figure 5

Team size and journals' rank Only a small proportion of papers authored by smaller teams are published in higher-ranked

journals and receive higher citations

Although larger teams publish papers that are on average cited more often, papers by smaller teams can also have high impact, and some of the highest impact papers are written by small teams. However, the probability that papers written by small teams have high impact is low. To explore the probability that a small team produces a paper with more impact than a large team, we examined the maximum number of citations after 2 years at the 70th, 80th, 90th, and 99th percentile. Given that the mean and median second-year citations for papers with 20 authors or more are 28.84 and 4, respectively, Figure 6 shows that to have a chance to outperform the median second-year citation of larger author papers, small teams have to be at the top 19.61st percentile. In other words, 80.39% of articles by smaller team authors receive at maximum less number of citations in their first 2 years than the median citations that papers with larger author teams receive during the same time span. The same is true for the journal rank score but to a lesser extent. To beat the median SJR value of larger teams (1.41), smaller team papers should be at the top 25.98th percentile. In other words, although smaller-team papers can achieve greater citation impact than the median larger-team paper, only a relatively small proportion do so. From an individual researcher's perspective, large-team papers tend to achieve recognition levels that smaller-team papers reach only at the highest end of their performance.

Figure 6 70, 80, 90, and 99 percentiles of small author groups for second-year citation and SJR

Large-team papers are consistently authors' more successful publications

To further explore whether authors should expect higher impact papers (in terms of citations and SJR) when they publish in small author teams or large author teams, we compared publications by authors in our dataset that were part of large (≥ 20) and small teams. We performed a dichotomous comparison of small-vs large-team outputs of the same author. In order to minimize the chance of repetition in small-teams records across all eligible authors, we used ≤ 5 as the definition for small teams. In total, we had 19508 eligible authors for citation metrics and 17884 authors for journal ranking. Figure 7 highlights that across different measures of impact, publications as part of a large team are consistently more successful for individual authors than their small-team publications. We also performed a one-sided test for each to assess and SJR (W = 216854610.5, CI = [0.517, ∞)) for small and large team contributions of all authors in this category). The median citation of publications of researchers as part of large teams was on average 36.52 higher after 2 years compared to their publications as part of small teams. For total citations and publication-date-corrected citations, the differences are 105.71 and 0.06, respectively. Similarly, the median SJR of large-team publications of researchers is on average 1.21 higher than their smaller group publications. We repeated the comparison with different definitions of large teams ( ≥ 15 and ≥ 25) which also yielded similar results (see Supplementary Materials).

Figure 7

Performance of smaller team project papers compared to larger team project papers of the same author

Citation counts are similar across reasons for large-team collaboration

In an exploratory analysis, we evaluated whether there is a difference in citation counts among the categories identified in the qualitative section. Due to the extreme overlap of papers with interdependencies (see Figure 2), it was not possible to perform pairwise comparisons.

However, considering all existing combinations separately, Figure 8 shows that no clear pattern is visible in median total citations of different categories. The variability is higher for secondyear citations, yet similarly, no clear patterns emerge.

Figure 8

Total citation and second-year citation counts across qualitative categories without overlap Considering the presence of individual categories separately (see Figure 9), however, 400 showed that papers in the Symbolic category had higher median total citation counts, whereas 401 this pattern was not apparent for second-year citations. This raises the question of whether the 402 citation advantage associated with large-team papers could be primarily attributable to papers in 403 the Symbolic category. To examine this possibility, we excluded Symbolic papers and calculated 404 the percentile that papers with fewer than 20 authors would need to reach to match the mean and 405 median total and second-year citation counts of the remaining large-team papers in our 406 qualitative sample. As shown in Table 1, even after excluding Symbolic papers, smaller-team 407 papers needed to rank relatively high within their citation distribution to reach citation levels 408 typical of the remaining large-team papers.

Figure 9

Total citation and second-year citation counts across qualitative categories with overlap

Discussion

Coordination is essential to address complex research questions in science. In response, many disciplines have increasingly organized themselves into larger research teams. Within psychology in particular, the growing culture of team science raises important questions about how such work is evaluated within existing reward structures, and whether these incentives support or discourage further growth in team-based research. This paper examined multiple aspects of the performance and impact of large-team papers in comparison to papers by small teams. We also provided a qualitative investigation of the underlying motivations for why researchers work in large teams in scientific papers.

In line with previous work, we found that large-team papers have been increasing in number, receive higher citation counts, and are published in higher ranked journals (Coles, 2024; Coles et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2019; Wuchty et al., 2007). Although such papers still represent a minority of all publications, their growth may partly reflect the shift in topics that attract researchers and journal editors in psychology. These projects can also offer researchers opportunities to work collaboratively, an aspect of academic research that many researchers value, and to expand their professional networks. It may also be due to an increased expectation from scientists to excel at skills like self-awareness, communication, and project management (Bennett & Gadlin, 2012), which could, in principle, encourage researchers to participate in larger team projects as a way to learn and apply these skills.

It is important to consider the context in which citation metrics are interpreted. Within the current academic reward structure, individual-level indicators such as citation counts, publications in highly ranked journals, and the rapid recognition of a researcher's work can influence career advancement (see Goring et al., 2014; Tiokhin et al., 2023). One reason for relying on such indicators may be that scientific quality is a complex and difficult concept to assess directly, highlighting the need for continued discussion about what constitutes quality and how it should be evaluated. Focusing on citation impact, our findings suggest that large-team papers tend to perform better than smaller-team papers. This raises a question about whether these indicators adequately capture contributions that are valuable to science and whether researchers should be incentivized to pursue them. This is a difficult discussion, as citations are correlated with scientific impact, but only as a proxy, and scientific research should not only have scientific, but also societal impact (for a discussion, see Isager et al., 2025). The extent to which citations should be valued is a complex discussion, but in general, scientists, funders, and scientific organizations currently assign some value to citations when evaluating the scientific contribution of scientists. As long as hiring, promotion, funding, and professional recognition continue to depend partly on citation metrics, researchers have incentives to perform well on them.

The value of citation impact and journal prestige may also differ across career stages.

Early-career researchers face particular pressure to establish themselves as independent scholars and develop a recognizable research profile (Bennett & Gadlin, 2012; Coles et al., 2022; Zucker, 2012). They may therefore hesitate to participate in large-team projects if having their contribution embedded within a long author list makes their individual contribution less visible, particularly when scientific credit is disproportionately attributed to principal investigators or other prominent contributors (Zucker, 2012). This creates a potential tension between the benefits associated with large-team outputs and the visibility of an individual researcher's contribution to those outputs. At the same time, early-career researchers may benefit from participating in large-team collaborations beyond having highly visible and highly cited publications. For example, participation in such projects may provide new opportunities, expand professional networks, offer access to support and mentorship, and expose researchers to new scientific perspectives, skills, and expertise (Zucker, 2012).

It is uncertain how hiring committees, or committee members of research proposals should evaluate the contributions that researchers made on small-team papers compared to largeteam papers to appropriately recognize their scientific contributions. Future research could examine how evaluators assess the CVs of early-career researchers with different combinations of small-and large-team publications, and whether these evaluations depend on citation impact, journal prestige, authorship position, or documented contributions. Such work could help establish whether the potential benefits of large-team participation identified here translate into career advantages for individual researchers or whether concerns about diluted credit offset these benefits. Narrative CVs, which allow scientists to describe the impact of their work, may provide evaluators with additional context and facilitate the recognition of a wider range of scientific contributions, such as contributions to team science.

The value of contributing to large-team projects may change once researchers have established an independent research profile. At later career stages, large-team publications may provide additional opportunities for visibility and recognition, as more senior scientists might benefit more from demonstrating leadership ability than demonstrating independence.

Anecdotally, we have seen how authorship on a large-team paper that was published in a highly ranked journal increased a researcher's visibility within their institution. Although these observations are anecdotal and should not be interpreted as evidence of a systematic career benefit, they illustrate one potential mechanism through which the citation and publication advantages associated with large-team research could translate into individual recognition. More generally, these competing considerations suggest that the incentives and potential returns associated with participating in large-team science may vary substantially across career stages.

A limitation of our analysis is that our results focus on citation counts and journal rank, neither of which informs us directly about the quality of the scientific knowledge that is produced. Moreover, it does not inform us about any possible causal mechanisms explaining the relationship between citation counts and team size. Although we do not make claims about the quality of the studies or the mechanisms behind this relationship, a considerable body of work has cautioned that citation counts and journal visibility do not reliably reflect research quality (Aksnes et al., 2019; Dougherty & Horne, 2022; Seglen, 1997). Several mechanisms can generate higher citation counts or publication in higher-ranked journals without necessarily reflecting differences in scientific quality. For example, the broader relevance of topics addressed by larger collaborations may increase their visibility and, consequently, their citation counts (Wu et al., 2019). Citation patterns may also be affected by social and cognitive biases.

Large collaborations frequently include more prestigious researchers and institutions, are often led by researchers from higher-resource countries, and typically involve larger samples (Coles et al., 2026). These characteristics may trigger authority-related biases and increase citations independently of research quality (Urlings et al., 2021). Citation counts may further be affected by self-citation (Aksnes, 2003), although the association between team size and citations has also been observed after accounting for self-citations in both our study and previous studies (e.g., Larivière et al., 2015). Network effects may also impact the citation count, as larger teams may have broader social and professional networks through which their work becomes visible and subsequently cited (Li et al., 2022). And indeed, our data extend these findings by showing how perspective and opinion pieces by large groups of authors gather a substantial number of citations.

Citation-based indicators are only one proxy for scientific impact. Alternative indicators include references to research in patents, policy, legal, or other non-academic documents, as well as measures of online attention, such as the number of times an article is saved, shared, or discussed on social media (Beerdsen, 2025; Brown, 2014; Velayos-Ortega & López-Carreño, 2023). However, these measures capture different dimensions of research influence, and each measure comes with its own limitations. Patent citations, for example, may be more informative in fields with direct technological applications and less generalizable to the social sciences, while policy, legal, and clinical uptake represent qualitatively different forms of societal influence that are difficult to combine into a single measure. Measures of online attention similarly capture visibility or engagement rather than necessarily reflecting research quality. Throughout this paper, we interpret citation counts specifically as an indicator of citation impact and SJR as an indicator of journal-level citation prestige. Our findings should be interpreted as evidence that large-team papers tend to receive greater scholarly citation attention and appear in journals with greater citation prestige, rather than evidence that large-team collaborations necessarily produce higher-quality science.

Through our qualitative analysis, we found that interdependencies were the most common reason for forming large teams. Among these, logistic and financial interdependencies were particularly frequent, which is consistent with the findings of Coles et al. (2026). This suggests that scaling up research (for example, by collecting larger samples or collecting data across multiple sites) is an important reason for large-team collaboration. This pattern may point to a mismatch between how research is conventionally organized and funded in psychology and the resources required to address increasingly ambitious research questions and methodological standards. Research funding is still often organized around individual PIs and their research groups and focuses more on novelty rather than what is required for further developing knowledge generation (Vaesen, 2026). However, researchers are expected to meet standards that require resources that exceed the capacity of a single investigator or laboratory. Large-team collaboration may provide one way of addressing this mismatch by pooling financial resources, infrastructure, access to participants, and scientific labour across researchers and institutions. In doing so, large teams may also make methodologically demanding research designs feasible by distributing the labour and resources required to implement them.

Our results also showed that the infrastructure created through large-team coordination can remain valuable beyond the project for which it was initially established. By establishing shared datasets, methodological standards, collaborative networks, and data-sharing mechanisms, large teams can create resources that can support future research. This was apparent in papers from our sample that relied on secondary analyses of data generated through large cohorts, clinical trials, or consortia. Although the analyses in these papers may not have necessarily required the same interdependencies as the original data collection, they relied on data that could only have been generated through substantial coordination. The scientific value of large-team coordination extends beyond its immediate outputs, with datasets and protocols providing resources for subsequent research. This also raises questions about co-authorship, as the data shared by large collaborations is often valuable for other scientific contributions, and was often collected at substantial financial or logistical costs. If subsequent research depends on the investments of a large collaboration, it might be important for fields to reflect on how they provide credit for the work that went into generating these rich datasets.

We also found that large teams can serve functions beyond addressing the interdependencies associated with complex empirical research. For example, some large-team publications in our sample were position papers, perspectives, commentaries, workshop reports, or research roadmaps. In these cases, the large number of authors may serve a signaling function, indicating broad support for a position, drawing attention to an issue, or representing consensus across a research community. These functions are not necessarily problematic. Establishing consensus and research priorities are important steps in scientific coordination (Rasti et al., 2026). A smaller subset of the papers we investigated did not reveal an apparent reason for the large number of authors. These categories raise questions about how individual contributions are defined and communicated. This may be due to social reasons for collaborations, such as benefiting from the increased visibility of the output, as mentioned by Jones (2021). It may also be a sign of honorary or gift authorship, which has been shown to occur in science (Gülen et al., 2020). A CRediT statement might help to transparently specify contributions of each author and prevent the impression of gift authorship. However, relatively broad categories in a CRediT statement do not necessarily communicate the magnitude or importance of each contribution, or the extent to which a particular contribution was necessary for the research. Research communities may therefore need to consider whether existing authorship conventions adequately distinguish between authorship reflecting direct contributions to a specific scholarly output and participation intended primarily to signal collective endorsement.

As long as recognition and reward procedures remain focused on individuals, improving coordination in science requires that the benefits of collaborative work be tangible for individual researchers. Our findings suggest that large-team collaborations are more likely to receive citation impact and visibility, often generate more immediate influence, and are on average cited more and published in higher-ranked journals than small-team papers by the same author.

Moreover, this study highlights that large-team collaborations primarily arise from the interdependencies and demands of complex research questions, but also from broader social and strategic factors. While coordinated research should ideally be driven by intrinsic scientific goals, making these additional motivators explicit may help increase the adoption of coordinated large-team research in scientific disciplines such as psychology. We need coordination to answer complex questions, and our results show that coordination is potentially rewarding in the current state of academia.
